# Selecting a critical circuit and its convex potential: exact finite-menu formulation

The product construction below is proved. The corresponding selected-circuit
bound for general compatible fibers is an open obligation in this search;
this note does not assume it, or a regularity/allocation interface at a
nonsmooth minimum.

## 1. Actual product theorem in arbitrary integer rank

Let P be a finite set of integer bases, K a d-simplex (d>=1), and S=P times K
with volume summed over fibers. Let g be the centroid of K. Suppose
Y=(p,g) is an actual global deepest point of raw depth Q and has a regular
nonvertical depth-attaining cap

    H={a dot(z-p)+u dot(x-g)>=0}, u!=0.             (1)

Regularity here means the cap-mass map is differentiable in the FULL
hyperplane parameters (A,b), with its usual coarea derivative, not merely
in normals constrained to pass through the original source. This permits
the simultaneous normal/threshold variation through a different point
used in strict contact. Proper/strictly-empty/strictly-full cuts on every
fiber are a sufficient condition. The finite symmetry group of K preserves
actual volume, halfspaces, and all fibers.

**Selection theorem.** There is a finite regular positive critical circuit
at Y and a nonnegative normal-dependent convex potential whose efficiency
for its response profile is at least Gamma_d. The circuit has at most d+1
rows after removing redundant normals. This is an existence statement,
not a claim about every old critical circuit.

Proof. Center coordinates at g, and let G range over the linear parts of
the affine vertex permutations of K. The image caps are

    H_G={a dot(z-p)+(G^(-T)u) dot(x-g)>=0}.          (2)

Every cap has raw mass Q and remains regular; its base coefficient is the
same a. The average of the G's and of their inverses is the zero linear
map, since every vector's permutation-orbit average is zero. Thus the
continuous normals in (2) positively balance. Caratheodory reduction
extracts a positive subcircuit of at most d+1 rows if desired.

Choose an exposed vertex e of conv(P) maximizing a dot z, so a dot(e-p)>=0.
Every selected cap at e contains its parallel through-g cap. An affine
function ell exposing e satisfies ell(e)=0 and ell(z)<0 on all other bases.
For a sufficiently large finite B, the potential

    Phi(n,z,x)=[n dot(x-g)+B ell(z)]_+

vanishes on every other actual fiber boundary and equals n dot(x-g) on
boundary K at e. It is nonnegative and convex in (z,x) for each fixed n.
Its denominator is d|K|. Each selected cap has numerator contribution at
least d times its parallel through-g cap volume, hence at least
 d Gamma_d |K| by ordinary Grünbaum. This is an inclusion argument; no
incorrect equality between an offset cap volume and its radial boundary
flux is used. Every normalized nonnegative weight choice on the selected
list consequently pays Gamma_d. In particular its normalized response
weights do. All halfspaces here are the actual oblique ambient caps.

If the source was originally specified as (p,y) with a regular positive
critical circuit, then y=g: permutation averaging gives (p,g) deepest;
regular strict-contact excludes any different deepest point from every
cap in the circuit, and positive continuous-normal balance excludes a
second deepest point in its fiber. This argument, including own-boundary
exclusion, is proved in
`candidate 567aa083fc8ee3ab`.

The theorem applies in any integer rank and does not require the deepest
bases to occupy all parities. It extends to a common fiber having a finite
volume-preserving affine symmetry group with zero average linear part.
It does not extend by assertion to varying fibers.

For the exact R4 product counterexample, starting with one canonical cap
and taking only continuous vertex permutations gives a common base tilt.
Its maximizing exposed fiber is strictly full in every new row; an
exposed-fiber potential has efficiency exactly 1. Thus its bad prescribed
profile of efficiency 40/93 does not obstruct favorable circuit selection.

## 2. Finite menus on arbitrary compatible fibers

Now let S be an actual finite full-fiber mixed convex family in arbitrary
integer and continuous dimensions, d>=1. Fix a deepest source Y=(p,y).
Take a finite menu of regular depth-attaining nonvertical caps through Y,
indexed j=1,...,N, with full normals (a_j,u_j), u_j!=0. Put

    S_j=sum_z H_(d-1)(K_z intersect boundary H_j)/||u_j||,
    b_j=S_j u_j.                                  (3)

Assume S_j>0, as holds when the own cut is proper. The vectors b_j are
unchanged by positive rescaling of a cap's defining equation. This
normalization is essential: theta below is the response profile weight,
not the unnormalized coefficient in the geometric normal balance.

The complete feasible set of response weights for this finite menu is

    T={theta in R^N:theta>=0, sum theta=1,
                              sum theta_j b_j=0}. (4)

Indeed a geometric positive circuit has coefficients rho_j with
sum rho_j u_j=0, and its response weights are proportional to rho_j/S_j.
Conversely a theta in (4) gives rho_j=theta_j S_j and the required positive
normal balance after deleting zero weights. Each selected cap still has
mass Q, and the selected list covers the entire source fiber plane.

Let eta be the sum over actual fibers of their (d-1)-dimensional boundary
Hausdorff measures, lifted to (n,z,x) using the outward continuous UNIT
normal n(x), defined almost everywhere. Let C be the cone of continuous
nonnegative normal-dependent potentials convex in physical variables.
Normalize Phi by integral Phi d eta=1. Define

    A_j(Phi)=integral Phi 1_Hj d eta,
    W_theta=sum theta_j 1_Hj,
    E_N=sup_(Phi in C, integral Phi=1)
              max_(theta in T) sum theta_j A_j(Phi).  (5)

If T is empty there is no regular circuit in this menu; no efficiency
conclusion follows. If it is nonempty, it is a compact polytope. For each
fixed Phi the inner maximum is attained at one of its extreme points.
Every extreme theta has at most rank{(1,b_j)}<=d+1 positive entries:
otherwise a nonzero dependence supported on those entries permits both
positive and negative small weight perturbations, contradicting extremality.
Thus the finite problem has the exact alternative form

    E_N=max_(theta an extreme point of T)
            sup_(Phi in C, integral Phi=1)
                 integral Phi W_theta d eta.      (6)

There are finitely many extreme points. Equation (6) uses only the fact
that a supremum commutes with a FINITE maximum; it makes no assertion that
the maximizing potential itself is attained.

The finite linear-program dual for the inner maximum is also exact:

    max_(theta in T) sum theta_j A_j
       =inf_(v in R^d) max_j [A_j-v dot b_j].       (7)

For example, this follows by introducing the scalar t with
 t+v dot b_j>=A_j in the ordinary equality-constrained finite LP dual.
Primal compactness gives a finite optimum; standard finite-dimensional LP
duality gives (7), including a rank-deficient span of the b_j. No minimax
exchange between Phi and v is asserted.

## 3. Quantifiers retained in the general search

For a fixed actual source, the unrestricted regular selection value is

    E_*(Y)=sup over finite regular critical menus with T nonempty of E_N.

The product theorem proves E_*(Y)>=Gamma_d by an explicit finite orbit.
The R4 and primitive-simplex examples prove that a UNIVERSAL assertion
about every prescribed critical profile is false. They do not prove
E_*(Y)<Gamma_d. Conversely the finite LP formulation supplies no lower
bound for E_*(Y) on arbitrary different fibers.

If an independently justified fixed-witness cover selects s sources,
and each selected source has E_*(Y_i)>=Gamma_d, then for every epsilon>0
one can select a finite circuit and a normalized potential Phi_i with
individual payment at least Gamma_d-epsilon. Since W_i>=0, their sum
Phi=sum_i Phi_i has denominator s and satisfies

    integral Phi W_i d eta / integral Phi d eta
             >=(Gamma_d-epsilon)/s for every i.   (8)

This is just the nonnegative summation lemma, with the choices made before
forming the sum. It neither asserts that all competing critical circuits
have these efficiencies nor supplies missing supporting-facet allocations.
The separate fixed-witness theorem supplies s<=k(I)<=k(P) under its stated
hypotheses. Any use at an attained shape minimum must still verify the
regularity/nonregular interface, persistence of the chosen finite cap
cover, and the actual variational sign conditions. Equation (8) alone
is not a proof of OC.

An unattained potential supremum is not an obstacle to a STRICT below-target
contradiction once all those interfaces are separately proved: choose
epsilon smaller than the given strict gap. It would be incorrect to turn
that observation into an assertion that a single exact-Gamma potential
always exists, or that the general selected-circuit lower bound has been
proved.

## 4. Exact affine fiberwise symmetry, with varying shapes or radii

The orbit argument does not require equal fibers. Here is its precise
stronger form. Let the actual positive fibers be

    K_z=c(z)+L_z,   c(z)=c0+Mz,

and suppose a finite group G of invertible linear maps satisfies

    G L_z=L_z for every map G and every base z,
    average_G G=0.                                (9)

All L_z are full-dimensional convex bodies. A finite linear group has
absolute determinant one in each element. Its orbit average is zero, so
invariance implies that each L_z has centroid zero. Thus c(z) is the
actual centroid of every fiber. Neither common volume nor common shape
is assumed.

The maps

    (z,x) -> (z,c(z)+G(x-c(z)))                    (10)

are genuine affine maps of the full ambient space. They preserve the
integer base, every actual fiber, mixed volume and halfspaces. The affine
hypothesis on c is essential to this assertion. They preserve regularity
of cap first variations as well.

At a deepest source with a regular critical circuit whose every row has
positive total coarea S_j, orbit averaging and strict contact as before
force the source to be (p,c(p)). The strict-contact proof only needs one
proper positive section somewhere in each row: that makes its total
coarea positive and ensures that raising its threshold removes mass. It
does not require the initially specified source to have an interior own
fiber cut. After orbit averaging and uniqueness, the source c(p) is of
course interior to its full-dimensional own fiber. Write one cap
in centered shear coordinates as

    a_tilde dot(z-p)+u dot(x-c(z))>=0.             (11)

Its whole group orbit has the common base coefficient a_tilde and
continuous normals G^(-T)u, which positively balance because the inverse
group has average zero. Select a positive subcircuit. Expose a vertex e
maximizing a_tilde dot z. Every selected endpoint trace contains its
parallel through-centroid cap at c(e).

The potential now is

    Phi(n,z,x)=[n dot(x-c(z))+B ell(z)]_+.          (12)

It is physically convex because c is affine. Since there are finitely
many bounded fibers, a single finite B localizes it to e. Its denominator
is d|K_e| and each numerator contribution is at least d Gamma_d |K_e|.
This proves the same favorable-circuit selection conclusion in every
integer rank, with varying fibers satisfying (9).

Two useful exact subclasses are homothetic simplex fibers on one affine
center graph, with arbitrary positive radii, and arbitrary centrally
symmetric fibers on one affine center graph, using G={I,-I}. In the latter
case each through-center cap has half the fiber volume, so the selected
circuit efficiency is at least 1/2. These are constructions of selected
critical circuits and potentials. The separate existing affine-center
OC theorems are not being claimed as newly resolved here.
